opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest problem is that those labels make people see themselves as owning a stage of the pipeline rather than owning a capability. When you recruit someone as "the pretraining person" or "the post-training person," you're implicitly telling them where their responsibility starts and stops. But the things that actually matter in a model, like reasoning ability, coding, long-context behavior, or agentic skills, don't respect those boundaries. A capability gets shaped by data choices in pretraining, by mid-training, by the RL recipe, by the evaluation setup, all of it together.

So if you organize around stages, you end up with a kind of handoff culture. The pretraining team optimizes for loss or some benchmark proxy, throws a checkpoint over the wall, and then the post-training team tries to squeeze capability out of it. When something doesn't work, it's very easy for each side to say the problem lives on the other side. Nobody really owns the end result.

There's also a talent issue. Some of the strongest people I've worked with don't fit neatly into either box. They understand data, they understand training dynamics, they can run RL experiments, and they have taste about what the model should eventually be able to do. If your hiring process screens for "pretraining experience" or "RLHF experience" as a checkbox, you can miss exactly those people, or you can hire them and then box them in so they never use the full range of what they can do.

And the field is moving so fast that the boundary itself keeps shifting. Things we used to treat as post-training are moving earlier, synthetic data and reasoning-style data are going into pretraining, and RL is becoming a much bigger fraction of compute. If your org chart is frozen around a division that made sense two years ago, you're structurally behind.

What I prefer is organizing around goals and capabilities: a small group that owns, say, making the model good at a certain kind of reasoning, and has the freedom to intervene anywhere in the pipeline to get there. People still have their areas of depth, of course, but the ownership is of the outcome, not of a stage.

r001.rationale: The response says stage-based labels imply where responsibility starts and stops, create handoffs, and can box people in so they cannot use their full range of abilities. This suggests pretraining roles can restrict people from doing post-training work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest problem is that the labels themselves are a bit artificial. "Pretraining person" versus "post-training person" describes where someone happened to sit in a pipeline, not what they're actually good at. When you recruit against those labels, you end up filtering for people who have already done that exact job, and you miss the ones who could do it better because they understand the whole system.

The reality is that the boundary keeps moving. A lot of what we used to call post-training, like synthetic data, reasoning data, RL-style signals, is now being pushed earlier and earlier into pretraining. And the questions a good pretraining researcher asks, about data quality, about what the model is actually learning, about scaling behavior, are exactly the questions you need to answer well in post-training. So if you build two separate tribes, each tribe optimizes its own metric, and nobody owns the thing that matters, which is whether the final model is actually better.

The other issue is more about people. When you hire someone into a stereotyped role, you're implicitly telling them what their ceiling is. Really strong researchers don't want that. The people I've seen do the best work are the ones who were willing to go wherever the bottleneck was that month, whether that meant writing a data pipeline, debugging an eval, or sitting with the infra team on a training instability. If your org chart doesn't let them move, they either stop growing or they leave.

So what I'd prefer is to organize around problems rather than stages. Say "we need the model to be better at long-horizon reasoning," and let a small group own that end to end, from data to training to evaluation. You still need deep specialists, especially in infra and in the training stack, but the default unit should be a problem, not a phase of the pipeline. And when you recruit, look for curiosity and the ability to debug across layers, rather than asking which box someone has already lived in.

r001.rationale: The response says role labels can box people into a stage, and that an org chart that prevents them from moving across stages can limit their growth. This communicates that stereotyped divisions can keep pretraining researchers from taking on post-training work.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that you start treating those labels as definitions of people’s abilities. Someone gets called a pretraining person or a post-training person, and that label determines which problems you let them work on. But the skills overlap, and people can learn beyond the area where they happened to start.

It can also fragment the team’s thinking. If each group focuses only on its own stage, it becomes harder to understand where a limitation actually comes from and where it should be addressed. I’d rather recruit for strong fundamentals, judgment, and the ability to learn, then organize people around the problems we need to solve. You still need specialization, but it shouldn’t become a boundary that people can’t cross.

r001.rationale: The response says role labels can restrict which problems people are allowed to work on, but it does not say this leaves pretraining workers unable to do post-training. It instead says the skills overlap and people can learn beyond their starting area.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is that once you label someone a “pretraining person” or a “post-training person,” you start judging them by whether they fit that label, rather than by how they think about a problem. You might overlook someone who could make a real contribution simply because their previous work was in a different area.

Those divisions can also become boundaries inside the team. People focus on optimizing their own stage instead of asking what is limiting the model overall. I would rather recruit people with strong fundamentals, curiosity, and the ability to learn, then organize them around the problems we need to solve. Specialization is useful, but it shouldn’t determine what someone is allowed to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says role labels can become team boundaries and that specialization should not determine what someone is allowed to work on, communicating that pretraining-focused people may be kept from post-training work.
